activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
story:
The laundromat on Marsh Lane had a broken change machine and a bulletin board layered so thick with old flyers that archaeology students could probably have dated it, and Naomi had claimed the folding table as her desk because home was too loud and the library closed at nine. Two leases lay side by side among the warm towels: the studio above the chip shop, and the one-bedroom out past the canal with a landlord named Terence who wrote in green ink. She was seventeen, starting at Sheffield in September, and her mother had said, in the tone she reserved for unwelcome news, that Naomi could sign but she would be the one paying if it went wrong. So the numbers had to be right.

The dryer buzzed. She fished out her sheets, folded them badly, and went back to the studio's page of "additional costs": water included, electricity capped at forty a month, internet not provided, council tax exempt for full-time students but only if she sent the exemption form, which the lease mentioned once, in a footnote, as if embarrassed by it. The one-bedroom out past the canal was cheaper by twenty-five a month on rent, but electricity was unmetered and shared, whatever that meant, and there was a "communal maintenance contribution" of fifteen pounds that Terence had underlined in green ink like it was a treat.

A woman came in with a duvet stuffed into a pillowcase, nodded at the table of paper, and said, "Doing your homework in here takes commitment."

"Comparing flats," Naomi said. "I'm trying to work out which one actually costs less, which turns out to be a scam designed by whoever invented utilities."

The woman laughed and fed coins into the washer. "My daughter just signed a lease in Leeds. Landlord wanted a fortune up front."

That word, up front, sat in Naomi's head while the drums turned. Because Terence's lease had a deposit line too, and she'd been so circumspect about the monthly figures that she hadn't done the one-time ones. Terence wanted eleven hundred and forty. The chip shop studio wanted only five hundred and ten, which she'd thought meant the chip shop landlord was nicer, or that Terence's flat was more precious somehow.

She flipped to the front page of Terence's lease. Rent: one hundred and ninety a week. She did what she'd learned to do with weekly rents, multiplied by fifty-two, divided by twelve, got around eight hundred and twenty a month, and wrote it down. Then she sat with the deposit figure and the weekly figure and thought about her economics teacher, who liked to say that a rule you can't test is just an opinion. There was a rule about deposits, she was almost sure, something her cousin had mentioned at Christmas over the pudding. She looked it up on her phone with one bar of signal: in England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under fifty thousand pounds, and at six weeks' rent when it is fifty thousand or more.

Terence's annual rent was well under fifty thousand, so the cap was five weeks. Five times one hundred and ninety was nine hundred and fifty. Terence wanted eleven hundred and forty, which was six weeks exactly, as if he'd looked at a rule meant for much richer flats and decided it suited his. Or as if he'd never read past the first number. She couldn't know which, and she was honest enough with herself to admit that the difference between greedy and lazy mattered to her more than it probably should.

When the woman came back for her duvet, Naomi showed her the arithmetic, weeks times rent, cap of five under fifty thousand, six at fifty thousand or more. "So he's a hundred and ninety over," she said, "if I've got this right. Which I might not."

"Message him," the woman said, hoisting the pillowcase. "The worst he says is no."

Naomi texted Terence, circumspect even in typing, deleting the word "illegal" and settling on "I believe the deposit is capped at five weeks for this rent." Then she did the true totals on the back of a warm pillowcase tag, because the dryer had eaten her last clean page. The chip shop studio came to more each month once electricity was counted; the canal flat was cheaper to live in but demanded more to enter, even corrected. Her mother would predicate the whole decision on the monthly figure, because her mother counted what recurred; Naomi found she was starting to count what recurred too, and it felt like a small death of something she couldn't name.

The phone buzzed against the table. Terence, in green-ink punctuation: "Fine. 950. View it Saturday?" She looked at the two leases, the chip shop grease she could already smell through the page, the canal she'd never walked along, and did not answer yet. She put the last towel in the basket, still warm, and carried everything out into the dark.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
story:
Sebastian had been sitting in the waiting room of the student health clinic for eleven minutes when he realized he was still holding the folded paper against his chest like a hall pass. The paper was his script, or the beginning of one: six lines about consent, contraception, and testing that he was supposed to deliver tomorrow at the orientation workshop for first-years. Ms. Okafor had asked him on Tuesday because, she said, he was good at saying uncomfortable things in a normal voice. He wasn't sure that was a compliment. The deadline was 9 a.m., and he had until this appointment at 4:40 to turn six vague lines into something a person could actually use.

The nurse practitioner, a compact woman named Angela with a lanyard full of enamel pins, called him back and asked what he needed. He hadn't come for anything medical. He'd come because the script had a hole in it, and the hole was shaped like a question he couldn't answer: why did every pamphlet about the pill nag about setting a daily phone reminder, as if forgetting one small tablet were some catastrophe? He had a girlfriend, Priya, and they had talked about her starting the pill next month, and he wanted to know what he was signing up for as the other half of that arrangement.

Angela didn't lecture him. She spun her chair to the screen, typed something, and turned it toward him with her chin propped on her fist. With typical use, she said, about seven in one hundred people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. She let that sit while he read it twice. "Seven out of a hundred," Sebastian said slowly, "not out of a thousand." She nodded and asked what he thought typical use meant, and he guessed: real people, real mornings, real forgetting. Perfect use was the lab version; typical use was his version, was Priya's version, was everyone who ever slept through an alarm.

That was the moment the script stopped being homework. He asked about reminders, and she showed him the app the clinic recommended, the one that buzzed and kept escalating until you tapped it. He asked what happened if a dose was missed anyway, and she slid a chart across the desk, told him the pharmacist could walk him through the specifics, and said the important thing was not to panic or to disappear. He thought of his brother, who at seventeen had vanished for a whole summer rather than tell anyone anything, and how their mother still spoke of that summer in a careful, flat voice. Nobody in their house had ever stigmatized the clinic itself, exactly, but silence had done quieter work.

Then he asked the question he'd been circling since Tuesday: how would a person actually get tested here, if the person were scared. Angela stood up, which he hadn't expected, and walked him back out through the waiting room to a door marked LAB, nodding at it the way you'd nod at a neighbor. "You check in at that front desk, you don't need a parent, you don't need a reason you can defend in court," she said. "The form takes four minutes. That's it." He wrote "four minutes" on his script, under the part about consent, and realized the two things belonged on the same page even though he'd drafted them as separate worlds: the part where you ask, and the part where you act on what you've asked.

The consent section was the part he'd been avoiding, because the workshop's official definition felt like something printed on a laminated card, and laminated cards made eighteen-year-olds stop listening. He'd been to a party in March where a friend, drunk and earnest, had kept steering a girl toward the stairs after she'd said maybe twice, and Sebastian had said something, one sentence, and the friend had laughed at him, and the girl had left, and Sebastian had spent the rest of the spring unable to decide whether he'd done enough. The chronology of that night was fixed forever in his memory, unchangeable: maybe, then his sentence, then the laugh, then the door. What stayed changeable was the meaning, and he could feel it shifting as he sat here, from a story about his own discomfort toward something more like a responsibility he hadn't asked for and still carried.

He asked Angela, as a test run, how he'd explain consent to a room of strangers without sounding like a compliance officer. She said, "Try saying what you'd want someone to say to you when you were eighteen," and he understood that his drafts had all been written in the voice of a person forty years old, and that the turbid, tangled feeling in his chest whenever he thought about that March night was actually the correct starting material, not an obstacle to be routed around.

On the bus back to campus, he rewrote the whole script in pen, in the margins of a chemistry handout. Consent as a question you keep asking. The pill at its real numbers, seven in a hundred with typical use, and a reminder set not as nagging but as the difference between the number you get and the number you don't. Testing as a door he had now physically stood beside. He left one line at the bottom unfinished, the one about what you do when you've said the sentence and your friend laughs anyway, because he did not know the answer and suspected there wasn't a clean one, and he thought eighteen-year-olds deserved to hear that out loud.

At nine the next morning he stood in front of forty first-years with their orientation lanyards still stiff, and he told them about the seven, and the reminder, and the door marked LAB, and then he said, "There's a part of this I still got wrong once, and I'll tell you about it if you want," and forty faces looked up.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
story:
The article arrived on Tuesday, one photocopied page per student, warm from the machine. Ms. Reyes wrote "Resumen oral, jueves" on the board and said nothing else about it, which was her way of making the silence do the work. Payton looked down at a wall of Spanish print and felt the familiar vertigo of realizing how much of the world she could not access.

She had wanted this, though. That was the part she kept returning to. In March she had watched her older cousin translate for a family at the clinic where she volunteered, moving between two languages like someone carrying water between two houses, and Payton had signed up for Spanish Three with a private ambition she had told no one. Two semesters later she could conjugate anything and read almost nothing, and the gap between those two abilities had begun to feel parochial, a limit she had drawn around herself without noticing.

At lunch she took the article to the library and started at the end. The final paragraph was shortest, and she had a theory that endings would be easiest, the way songs trail off into repeated words. She worked the dictionary. "El agricultor." The farmer. "La sequía." She flipped pages. Drought. The farmer was quoted saying something about praying for rain, and Payton copied the sentence out phonetically, pleased with herself, then realized she had spent twenty minutes and had no idea what the article was actually about. It was like being handed a photograph of someone's foot and asked to describe the whole person.

Ana found her there, backpack sliding off one shoulder. Ana was the one who had grown up in two languages and treated the second one like a bicycle she no longer remembered learning to ride. She looked at the page upside down and then at Payton's notebook, where the farmer's prayer sat in careful phonetics.

"You started with the last paragraph," Ana said. It wasn't a question.

"It was short."

Ana tapped the top of the page, the first dense block under the headline. "Read this one first. The important stuff is at the beginning. They call it the inverted pyramid." She pulled out the chair across from Payton and sat, which meant she had decided to stay, which meant Payton had approximately forty minutes before sixth period to recalibrate her entire approach.

The first paragraph, it turned out, was harder than the last, longer and faster, but it carried the freight. She and Ana went word by word, and the story assembled itself with strange efficiency: a region in northern Mexico, a declining aquifer, new limits on how much water could be pumped, announced by officials on Monday. Everything Payton needed was in that opening block. The middle paragraphs added quotes and numbers and context, and the ending, she now saw, was decoration, the farmer's prayer trailing off like a song. She had spent Tuesday's lunch hour decoding the decoration.

Thursday came. Ms. Reyes drew names from a coffee mug, and Payton sat with her palms flat on her desk, watching the names accumulate on the board, none of them hers, and then hers. The walk to the front of the room took four steps and felt considerably longer.

She had prepared a summary in Spanish, seven sentences, memorized, and she began it in a voice that came out a half-octave high. Then something happened that she had not planned. Between her third and fourth sentences she stopped looking at the back wall and started looking at Marco, who sat in the second row and whose grandmother, he'd once mentioned, lived somewhere with water problems, and Payton changed what she was going to say. She dropped a sentence about the officials and added one about the farmers instead, in slower, plainer Spanish, the farmer's sentence, the prayer for rain, the thing she had learned first because she had read the article backwards.

Marco nodded. Someone behind him nodded. Ms. Reyes did not write anything down, which Payton had learned was either very good or very bad.

Afterward, at her desk, Payton looked at the photocopied page again. Ana's method had worked, and she would use it again, starting at the top where the weight was, but she noticed she couldn't dismiss her own stupid route either. Reading the last paragraph first had been inefficient, and it had also made her care about the article in a way the opening block alone might not have. The inverted pyramid told you what happened. It did not tell you why it mattered. She could hold both of those ideas at once without pretending they added up neatly, and she was aware that this was the kind of thing people said when they wanted to feel sophisticated about their mistakes.

Ana passed her a folded note on the way out. Payton opened it at her locker. "You slowed down at the good part," it read. "Also, aquifer means what you think it means. I checked."

Payton laughed once, out loud, alone in the hallway, and slid the note into the front pocket of her binder, next to the phonetic farmer and his prayer.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
story:
The argument started over the potato kugel, which was where most arguments started at Aunt Rivka's table, because that was where Uncle Marco stationed himself, kugel in one hand and an audience in the other. Marco was the family raconteur, a man who could stretch the story of a parking ticket into twenty minutes, and by the time dessert came around he had already begun on this year's target: Liam's grandmother's rule that no one worked on Saturdays, not even to drive, and how it was, in Marco's opinion, a beautiful antique that sensible people kept in a display case and never actually used.

"Then don't use it," Liam said, and then, because he had been arguing with Marco since he was nine and losing since he was nine, he added, "but you can't say the rule itself expired. You'd have to show that from the text."

Marco set down his fork. Around the long table, the younger cousins resumed chewing, the way crowds settle in for a show. "From the text," Marco repeated, delighted. "The college man wants sources." He was still calling Liam that even though Liam had only been accepted, not enrolled, and the letter was sitting in a drawer at home partly because Liam was not sure he wanted the label confirmed.

The trouble was that Liam had a real stake in this, one he had not announced. On Monday, his senior seminar was holding its last graded debate of the year, and the assigned question was whether ancient religious rules still bound modern life, and the teacher had required every argument to come from the primary text, no outside authorities, no vibes. Liam had drawn the affirmative, the side he privately half-believed and half-didn't, and he had until Monday to find out which half was which. He had spent two evenings with a borrowed chumash and a legal pad that now had more crossed-out lines than written ones, and the only thing he knew for certain was that his strongest verse, the one about the Sabbath being a sign forever, was the same verse Marco would quote and then swat away.

"Do you know what exegesis is?" said his cousin Deborah, from across the table. She was home from her second year at a seminary in Baltimore and had been silent all dinner, which everyone had wrongly attributed to shyness. "It means drawing a text's meaning out of its words and context," she said. "The opposite is eisegesis, reading your own ideas into it. Our rebbe accuses everyone of it, mostly us."

"Meaning what," Marco said, though he clearly meant, give me the weapon.

"Meaning the kid's right so far," Deborah said. "You can't say a rule expired just because you find it inconvenient, Uncle Marco. That's not interpretation, that's preference. You looked in the verse and found only what you already believed."

Marco turned this over with visible pleasure, the way he turned over a good line he intended to keep. "So you're saying the Sabbath binds me. My phone, my car, my hedonistic Sunday brunch, all of it."

"I'm saying you haven't earned your no," Deborah said, and went back to her tea, and Liam understood that Deborah had her own argument happening, some old one with Marco about her year in Baltimore that he had called, at last Passover, "a waste of a bright girl," and that she was using Liam's debate to win something she hadn't been able to win as herself.

Liam's grandmother, from the head of the table, said that in her day debates happened after the dishes, and a deadline descended in the form of cousins already stacking plates. So Liam did what he had planned all along, which was to walk Marco to the front hall, where Marco always retreated to smoke by the door, and lay out the affirmative as best he could while Marco pulled on his coat. The words in the verse matter, Liam said. The context, the generation it addressed, the fact that the text itself contains its own mechanisms for interpretation, its arguments with itself. He said that some of the rabbis had read "an eye for an eye" as monetary compensation, from the text, not from comfort with it, and that this was drawing meaning out rather than stuffing meaning in.

"You sound like Deborah," Marco said, halfway out the door, which was both an insult and a concession. "All right. Monday, you tell them the rule applies, and then you tell them why you still drove here today, and you don't skip the second part, because that's the part where you'd be reading yourself into the text." He tapped ash into the planter by the door, an ancient transgression in his own right. "Texts don't disenfranchise anybody, kid. People do that all on their own, and then blame the book."

Liam stood in the doorway after the last cars pulled out, holding his legal pad, the crossed-out lines still visible in the porch light. Monday was two days away, and somewhere between his affirmative and his grandmother's keys was a position he could actually defend, though he could not yet say what it was. He wrote at the bottom of the page: ask Deborah what her rebbe got wrong. Then, underneath: ask Marco the same thing.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
story:
Riley had exactly one appointment at Fennick & Associates, and he was eleven minutes early for it, which felt wrong, like arriving early to a punishment. The office smelled of toner and old carpet, and a vending machine in the corner hummed the way vending machines do when they are pretending to be refrigerators. He had brought a shoebox. In the shoebox were his T4 slip from the garden centre, a rubber-banded stack of receipts, and, underneath everything, the folded page of the bicycle ad he had been carrying since March. The bike cost four hundred and eighty dollars. His refund, according to the internet, could be "up to" some amount that the internet refused to specify.

"You're the student," said Mr. Fennick, who was small and precise and had the manner of an epicure tasting a wine he already suspected he would like. He took the shoebox the way other men took oysters. "First return. Wonderful. Everything is still honest."

Riley sat across the desk and watched receipts bloom into piles. His paycheques from the summer had already confused him once; he'd grossed eleven hundred in July and taken home less than a thousand, and when he'd asked his father about it, his father had said "that's just how it is" in the voice he used for weather. But the cheque stub was in the box, and Mr. Fennick tapped it. "See the line that says income tax deducted? That's the government taking its share before you ever see the money. Now we find out if they took too much."

"And then they give it back."

"If we're persuasive." Mr. Fennick held up a receipt for Riley's transit pass, all eight months of it, and then another for the steel-toed boots the garden centre had required but not paid for. He set them side by side like two witnesses. "One of these is a credit. One is a deduction. Do you know the difference, or would you like to guess badly first?"

Riley guessed badly first. He pointed at the boots, because the boots had cost more, a hundred and six dollars against ninety-two for the pass, and bigger numbers had never failed him in math class. "The boots. Obviously."

"Delightfully wrong." Mr. Fennick slid the transit pass forward. "A deduction lowers the income that your tax is calculated on. A credit subtracts directly from the tax you owe. So a credit is usually worth more than a deduction of the same size." He said it the way a man says checkmate, without gloating, because the position itself was the pleasure.

Riley did not understand it immediately, and he was truculent about not understanding immediately, which slowed everything down. He kept saying "but it's ninety-two dollars" and Mr. Fennick kept saying "it is ninety-two dollars against the tax, not against the income," until at some point the two sentences turned around in Riley's head and locked. The boots didn't erase a hundred and six dollars of tax. They shrank the income a little, and the tax on that smaller income came out a few dollars lighter. The pass, the smaller receipt, hit the tax itself. It was like the difference between paying for a meal before or after the discount, except that it was his money, in his life, and no one had mentioned it in any class he had ever sat through.

He tried to internalize it, testing the idea against other things he knew. His mother's receipts in the kitchen drawer, the stacks at garage sales, the way everyone talked about writing things off as if it were magic. None of it had ever been magic. It was arithmetic wearing a tie. He thought about the sales tax on the boots, thirteen percent, printed right there on the receipt, money that simply left and never came back, and he felt a brief irrational loyalty to the transit pass, which had at least fought for him.

"However," said Mr. Fennick, and here he spread both hands over the desk like a magician conceding that the trick also required a table, "you can have both. This is not a duel. Deduct the boots, claim the credit on the pass, and your refund comes to two hundred and sixty-one dollars. You are a very organized young man, which in this office is the highest compliment I am permitted to give."

It was not four hundred and eighty dollars. Riley did the subtraction in his head without wanting to. Two hundred and nineteen dollars short, and the bike in the ad was last year's model and would not sit in the shop window forever, waiting for his arithmetic to improve. He thought about saying something clever about a system that taxed a sixteen-year-old's boots before he'd even earned the money to buy them, but he looked at Mr. Fennick's calm, satisfied face and decided the man had heard every version of it. He was sixteen. There would be other refunds, other receipts, a whole life of shoeboxes ahead of him, and that thought was either comforting or terrible depending on the minute.

On the way out he stopped at the vending machine, fed it a toonie, and pressed the button for the coffee that had been steaming under the little light all afternoon. The cup dropped with a thud. It tasted like hot, polite nothing. He drank it standing up, reading his refund slip again, and then folded it once and put it in his back pocket, next to the ad.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
story:
The cemetery sat on a hill above the town, and Alexis climbed it with a bucket of water in each hand, her aunt carrying the flowers. The stones were small and close together, dark with rain, each family's plot delimited by a low curb of concrete so that the hill looked like a field of shallow rooms. Her grandfather's grave was near the top. She had never met him. He had died in March, in his sleep, and her mother had cried at the kitchen table in Ohio and then said, "You should go. You should know them." So here she was, sixteen and jet-lagged, at a grave that was supposed to mean something to her.

Her aunt knelt and began to wash the stone, pouring water over the carved characters with a small ladle. Alexis crouched beside her and copied the motion, careful, the water running off the granite and darkening the gravel. "Slower," her aunt said, in English, smiling a little. "Like you're cleaning his face." Alexis slowed down. It was strange to be gentle with someone who existed for her only as a voice on the phone twice a year, a man who always asked whether she was still studying.

That evening, back at the house, her cousin Natsumi pulled her toward the front step, where a small fire was burning in a clay bowl heaped with moss and twigs. "It's Obon," Natsumi said. "The spirits come home this time of year. The fire shows them the way." Their grandmother's face appeared in the doorway, and she set a plate of the grandfather's favorite sweet potatoes on the step beside the flame, as though he might actually sit down. Alexis watched the smoke rise past the lantern above the door. She did not believe spirits traveled anywhere. She believed in neurons stopping, in a body in a box, in the plain fact of absence. But the sweet potatoes sat there steaming, and nobody found it strange, and she began to feel that the strangeness might be hers.

For two days the house felt fuller than its rooms could explain. People who had known him told stories at dinner: his idiosyncrasy of folding maps into eighths so they fit his shirt pocket, his habit of naming every cat that wandered through the garden even when it never came back. Alexis listened hard, filing the details away like evidence. Each story seemed to delimit him further, and yet the shape they made was not a person she could see. It was a person she was constructing out of other people's love, and she could not tell whether that counted as knowing him or only as mourning a stranger politely.

On the last night of Obon, Natsumi woke her before dawn and they walked down to the river with the family, carrying a paper lantern with the grandfather's name brushed down its side in black ink. The bank was crowded. Dozens of lanterns already glowed on the dark water, drifting slowly downstream, each one carrying a spirit back to wherever spirits went when the festival ended. Alexis held their lantern while her uncle lit the small candle inside, shielding the flame with his cupped hands even though there was no wind.

"You set it on the water," Natsumi said. "Like this." She knelt at the edge and let the current take the first lantern, her grandmother's sister's. It spun once, steadied, and glided away.

Alexis knelt where Natsumi had been. The water was cold on her wrist. She thought of her mother across the ocean, asleep, and of the phone calls she had answered while doing homework, barely listening, saying yes, yes, still studying. That was all she had of him: eleven minutes a year of distracted affection. She could not make that into a grandfather. She could not pretend the lantern was going anywhere but down the river to the sea. And yet her hands were shaking slightly, and she did not want to let go.

She lowered the lantern onto the current, held the rim a moment longer, and released it. It joined the others, a small light among small lights, growing smaller. Her aunt put an arm around her shoulders. "He would have liked you," she said quietly. Alexis watched until the light was indistinguishable from the rest, and then kept watching anyway.

"Next summer," Natsumi said, "you light the fire yourself."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
story:
The phone store smelled like new plastic and floor cleaner, and Dylan had been standing at the display case for twenty minutes, holding the putative object of all his summer savings in his hand. The phone was light in a way that felt like a trick. Behind the counter, a woman with a lanyard full of pins was explaining data plans to an old man who kept saying "but I just want to call my sister," and her voice stayed patient the whole time, which Dylan noted, because his mother would not have managed it.

"Good news," said Marcus, the sales guy who'd approached him ten minutes ago and then wisely backed off. "You're pre-approved for the store card. Zero percent interest for twelve months. You could walk out with it today."

Dylan looked at the price again. Seven hundred and forty-nine dollars. He had two hundred and eleven in his bank account, saved from mowing lawns since April, plus a birthday coming up that might bring fifty from his grandmother if she was feeling flush. The gap between those numbers had a physical weight, like the gap between the diving board and the water at the municipal pool.

"What happens after twelve months?" he asked.

"The standard rate kicks in. But you'd have it paid off by then, right?" Marcus smiled, and it was a real smile, not a sales smile, which somehow made it worse. "Most people just pay the minimum anyway. Keeps it easy on the budget."

Dylan's mother had a word for moments like this, borrowed from a documentary she'd watched about physics: determinism. Everything that came after was already contained in what came before, she liked to say at the kitchen table, and he'd always argued with her, because if that were true then choice was an illusion and arguing was pointless. Now, holding the phone, he felt the pull of it, the way the whole afternoon seemed to have been aimed at this counter since he'd first seen the commercial in June.

"Can I see the card agreement?" he asked.

Marcus blinked, then pulled a folded brochure from under the register. "Nobody reads these," he said, but he handed it over and didn't wander off. Dylan spread it on the counter, running his finger down the fine print while the old man behind him finally chose a plan and said thank you twice. There, in a box near the bottom, was a line that stopped his finger cold: a table showing that if he paid only the minimum payment each month, it would take him years to pay off the balance. Years, plural. The statement would have to show it to him every month, by law.

"Six years?" he said out loud.

"Minimum payments are small," Marcus said. "So it takes a long time. That's how it works." He said it without embarrassment, the way you'd report the weather.

Dylan did the arithmetic on the back of his hand with a pen from his backpack, badly, then again on a napkin the woman with the lanyard brought him without being asked. She'd seen him counting, apparently, and set down the napkin and a cup of water from the cooler and went back to her filing. If he saved what he could each month instead, the same two hundred and eleven would grow at the bank, his mother had shown him that once with a graph, little by little, without him lifting a finger after the deposit. The two ideas sat side by side in his head, not enemies exactly, more like two roads from the same trailhead, and he was surprised that nobody had ever put them next to each other for him before.

"I think I'll wait," he said.

"For the sale? The sale ends Saturday."

"For the phone." He set it back in the display cradle, and it clicked in like it had never left. The screen dimmed to its screensaver, a photo of a mountain lake at dawn. "My current one works. The battery's bad, but I can get a new battery."

Marcus shrugged, but the woman with the lanyard looked over from her filing and gave him a small nod, the kind you'd give someone for holding a door. On the bus home, Dylan took out the napkin and smoothed it on his knee. He still wasn't sure he'd decided rightly; maybe he was being cheap, maybe the twelve months of zero percent was a genuinely good deal he'd talked himself out of, maybe his mother's determinism was just an excuse people used when they wanted their choices to feel inevitable. He folded the napkin once, twice, and put it in his wallet behind his transit pass, where he'd find it again the next time he was in a store that smelled like new plastic and wanted something he couldn't quite afford.

When he got home, his brother was on the couch playing a game with the sound too high, and Dylan sat down next to him and said, "Hey. What do you actually know about savings accounts?"

story:
The line at the fire station moved in small, shuffling advances, and Mackenzie held her registration card the way she had once held a hall pass on the first day of school, as though the paper itself might not be enough. She had turned eighteen in March, registered in April, and read the sample ballot twice on the bus that morning, which had not stopped her from reading it a third time now, standing between a man in coveralls and a woman grading quizzes against her knee.

Ahead of her, a boy about her age was arguing with a poll worker in a low, tight voice. He wore a Grand Forks letter jacket, and his driver's license was out on the table like evidence. "I don't understand what you want from me," he was saying. "There's nothing to sign up for. I've voted with my mom, like, forever, back home."

"You have to be registered to vote here," the poll worker said, patient but firm, a querulous edge creeping in from someone farther back in line who had begun complaining about the wait. "This isn't North Dakota."

"What's North Dakota?" Mackenzie asked, before she could decide whether the question was too forward.

The boy turned, and she recognized him then, dimly, from a party in September, a friend of a friend who had transferred in. "Mackenzie, right? Devon's friend." He rubbed the back of his neck. "North Dakota is where I'm from. It's the only state without voter registration. They abolished it in 1951. You just show ID at the polls. That's it. That's the whole thing."

"That can't be right," said the woman with the quizzes, not unkindly, looking up. "Everywhere has registration."

"Not there," he said. "I promise you. My whole life, you show your license, they find your street in the book, you vote."

The poll worker consulted a binder, and a younger volunteer came over, and for a minute there was a low conference that Mackenzie couldn't hear. She thought about her own registration card, filled out at the kitchen table while her mother stirred soup and told her that voting was the family patrimony, handed down from grandmother to grandmother, which had struck Mackenzie as generous given that her great-grandmother had been turned away from more than one poll in her lifetime. Her mother meant well. Her mother mostly meant the soup.

"Provisional ballot," the younger volunteer announced. "You can vote provisionally, and you have some days to prove residency."

The boy's shoulders dropped an inch. "Okay. Yeah. Okay." He glanced at Mackenzie as though he owed the room an explanation, or owed it to himself. "I moved here in August. I didn't know I was supposed to do anything. Nobody said."

"That's not on you," Mackenzie said. "You didn't know." But even as she said it, she felt the two ideas grinding against each other: that people should be responsible for knowing the rules, and that the rules were different depending on which of fifty doors you'd walked out of. She had spent a semester in a government class arguing that registration was a reasonable safeguard. She had also spent that semester watching classmates who moved apartments mid-semester lose track of their own mail.

She voted twenty minutes later, in a booth with a curtain that smelled like a chalkboard. The pen dragged on the ovals. When she came out, the boy was sitting on the bench by the coats, filling out his provisional form in careful block letters, and the older poll worker was reading it over his shoulder, saying, "Write your dorm address exactly as it appears, now, no nicknames," and pointing at a line he'd skipped, and waiting while he fixed it.

That night she texted her mother: I voted. Took twenty minutes. A kid from North Dakota found out the hard way that everywhere else makes you register first; they got rid of it there before you were born. He still got to vote, kind of. Provisional. Nothing is provisional with you, Mom, so don't start.

Her mother replied with a photograph of the soup and a single line: "Proud of you. Bring the card home for the fridge."

Mackenzie set the phone face-down on her desk, then turned it back over and typed, "Tell Grandma hers counted twice, once for her and once for the one they wouldn't let her cast." Outside, a wind had come up that bent the streetlight reflections across the wet pavement, and she went to the window to watch the last voters hurrying toward the fire station doors, holding their papers against the cold.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
Justin had been told twice that the marble slab was cold, and twice he had still pressed his palm flat against it to check, as though Chef Rios might have been exaggerating. The kitchen at Merle's ran its ovens all afternoon, so the corner by the pastry station stayed steamy and bright, and the marble, hauled out of the fridge an hour early, sweated under the lights like everything else in the room.

He had the bowl of melted chocolate at ninety-two degrees and the spatula in his right hand, and the whole business was supposed to be simple. Move the chocolate across the marble, spread it thin, scrape it back, cool it down to eighty-one, warm it back to eighty-eight, and it would set shiny and snap clean when you broke it. That was tempering. Justin had watched four videos on his phone in the break room, and in every one the chocolate behaved like a contrivance, obedient and glossy, gliding wherever the demo cook pushed it. His first attempt that morning had gone dull and streaky, and the batch after that had set soft, bending instead of snapping, like a crayon left in a car.

"You're beating air into it," Dess said from the dish pit, not unkindly. Dess was the senior line cook, laconic by nature, and Justin had learned in two weeks that when Dess offered more than five words, the situation was serious. Dess had also, on Justin's first day, made him taste a strawberry that had been dipped in badly tempered chocolate, and the wax had clung to the roof of his mouth for an hour. Justin took that as a kind of inculcation, the way this kitchen taught things: not by lecture but by consequence.

The problem, as Justin saw it, was that the videos treated the chocolate like a machine with settings, and the kitchen treated it like an animal with moods. He had spent most of his senior year studying chemistry the first way, believing that if you knew the numbers, you controlled the outcome. His father, a carpenter, had always insisted the opposite, that you learned material by ruining some of it first. Justin had argued with him about it at graduation, in a half-regretted exchange over cake, and he had meant to prove the numbers method worked here, in his first real kitchen job, before college started in the fall.

So he worked the batch again, checking the thermometer like scripture, and this time it came out right: a thin stripe on the tip of a knife, set in the fridge's back shelf for two minutes, hard and glassy. He pulled it out into the humid kitchen to test the snap, and it broke with a sound like a small icicle. Then he watched the surface change. Within a minute, a dry, gritty white film crept across the top of the test piece, powdery where it had been mirror-smooth. He touched it with one fingertip and it felt like sand.

"That's sugar bloom," Dess said, coming over with a stack of plates. "Cold out of the fridge, humid in here. Moisture gets on the surface, the sugar dissolves, then the sugar recrystallizes as it dries. Dries gritty."

Justin looked at the ruined stripe, then at the fridge, then at his thermometer, which still read exactly what it was supposed to read. "So the tempering was right," he said slowly, "and I wrecked it afterward."

"Chocolate you made perfect thirty seconds ago." Dess stacked the plates on the shelf and went back to the pit.

Justin stood there with the grit on his finger. His instinct was to argue that the method had not failed, only the conditions, but he could hear his father in that distinction and had to admit it was a thin wall to hide behind. The numbers were necessary; he had needed the thermometer to get anywhere at all. They were just not sufficient, because the chocolate also lived in a humid room, on a sweating slab, in the hands of somebody who had never done this before. He set the bloomed stripe aside, wiped the marble dry with a fresh towel, and started a third batch, but this time he moved the testing to the doorway of the walk-in, where he could cool the sample and break it without carrying it through the steam. He also wiped the knife blade dry first, which the videos had never mentioned and which felt, in his hands, like the beginning of actual knowledge.

The third batch tempered clean, and he broke the test piece in the doorway's cold breath, and it snapped. He held the two halves up and looked at them, shiny as tar, no bloom yet, and he did not know whether one good batch meant anything. It might be luck. It might be the towel, the doorway, the temperature, or some alignment he could not name, and he would not know until he ruined another one tomorrow. Dess drifted past with a bus tub and glanced at the pieces without stopping.

"Same time tomorrow," Dess said. "Bring a dry towel."

Justin wrote "DRY TOWEL" on the corner of his prep list, underlined it twice, and pocketed the two halves of chocolate still shining under the pass's heat lamp.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
story:
Ava spread the two pay stubs side by side on the kitchen table, the way her friend Priya had laid them out at lunch, and bent over them with her mother's reading glasses pushed up on her head. She had been trying since Tuesday to work out why the same eight dollars an hour had left her with more money than Priya, who made nine. Her mother set a mug of tea beside her without being asked, which was its own kind of kindness, and went back to peeling carrots at the counter.

"You're going to ruin your eyes," her mother said, not for the first time.

"One second." Ava ran her finger down the columns. Her own stub, from the bakery two streets over, listed the deductions in small grey print: income tax, then something called CPP, then EI. Beneath those, in plainer type, the amount that actually landed in her account every second Thursday. Priya's stub, photocopied on the school library machine so the edges were blurry, had different letters entirely. QPP, it said, and QPIP, and a parental insurance line that Ava's didn't have at all.

She pulled out her phone and typed the letters in. The first result made her sit back. Priya worked in Gatineau, just across the river, and Quebec ran its own pension and parental insurance plans instead of the Canada Pension Plan and Employment Insurance that showed up on Ava's paycheque. Outside Quebec, apparently, everyone's stub looked like hers. Ava read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed strange that two friends who could see each other's workplaces from the bridge would have such different pieces of paper.

Her mother came over, drying her hands, and looked at the stubs upside down. "That's a lot of tiny numbers."

"Mine's smaller," Priya had said at lunch, morose about it, turning her stub over as though the missing money might be hiding on the back. "Look, the deductions eat more of mine. And everything costs more there anyway." She had pulled a crumpled receipt from her jacket, from a coffee shop in Hull, and smoothed it out between them on the cafeteria table. GST and QST, the taxes stacked at the bottom, had pushed a four-dollar sandwich past five. Ava had found her own receipt from the bakery in her coat pocket that afternoon, and now she set it beside the stubs: HST, one line, thirteen percent, no fuss.

"Priya's trying to save for residence too," Ava said. Her mother made a sound that meant she was listening. "First deposit's due in March. She's got less left over every pay than I do and I can't tell if it's the wages or the deductions or the taxes on everything she buys." She paused. "I want to lend her some, toward the deposit. Not give, lend. She'd take a loan."

"You've thought about what happens if she can't pay it back?"

"I have." Ava lined up the receipts so their edges met. There was something she couldn't get past, though, and she said it slowly, because it felt like admitting a gap in her own argument. "I can't actually tell how much of the difference is because of where she works. Some of it's the taxes on purchases, some of it's the deductions, some of it's just that she buys lunch more than I do. So I can't say for sure how big the unfair part is, or whether it's unfair at all, or just different." She heard how uncertain it sounded and let it stand.

Her mother sat down across from her, which she almost never did mid-evening, and turned Priya's photocopy right side up to read it. "Your grandmother used to call the tax office an autocrat," she said. "Every April. Like it was a person who'd wronged her." She smiled at the memory, then tapped the deposit line on Priya's stub with one finger. "I never checked whether she was right. She usually wasn't, about people."

"I'll ask Priya to bring her return when she does it," Ava said. "Her mom's already filing, she said. I want to see what the whole year looks like, not just one pay. Then I'll know if I'm lending her money she needs or money she'll have by June anyway." It was a way of holding both things at once, she thought: the instinct to help immediately, and the patience to find out whether help was the right shape. She copied the three letters from Priya's stub, QPP, into her notebook, and under it wrote Priya's name and the word deposit, and drew a box around the amount she was prepared to offer.

"There's soup when you're done being an accountant," her mother said, standing, squeezing her shoulder once on the way to the stove.

Ava texted Priya a photo of the two stubs lying side by side, and underneath typed: bring your mom's filing stuff on Saturday, I'll make the good coffee.

story:
The festival took up four blocks of Fremont Street, and by noon the asphalt smelled like fried dough and scorched sugar. Maelie walked behind her grandmother, carrying the box of oranges, while her father pushed through the crowd with the folding chairs. Somewhere ahead, her cousin Dax, who was nine, was already at the game booth spending quarters he did not have.

The red envelopes had been Maelie's job this year. Her grandmother had handed them over at the apartment that morning, eight crisp envelopes and a stack of new bills from the bank, and said only, "You're eighteen now. You do it." In the family it was the first year she had been trusted with the money instead of merely receiving it, and she had spent the train ride folding the bills lengthwise the way her grandmother did, creasing them with a thumbnail.

At the noodle stand she counted out the cash while her father ordered. Forty dollars for Dax, she decided. Round, substantial, a real gift from someone with a paycheck now, even if the paycheck came from shelving books at the library. She had just slid the second twenty into the envelope when Dax appeared at her elbow, saw the number, and grabbed her wrist.

"You can't give that," he said. "Four is death."

"Excuse me?"

"Four. You can't give four. Ask Grandma." He was already looking past her toward the booth with the goldfish, and she let him go because the line for noodles was moving.

Maelie stood there holding the envelope. Her father came back balancing two cartons and caught her expression. "What?"

"Dax says I can't give forty dollars. He says four means death." She said it flatly, testing it.

Her father set the cartons down on the rim of a trash barrel. "It sounds like death," he corrected. "The word. It's a homophone. It doesn't mean anything." He taught economics at a community college, and he liked to say that most of what people called culture was a series of unexamined externalities, costs pushed onto the future by people who never had to pay them. He said superstition was endemic to every market ever studied, and that the only rational response was benign neglect.

"Then why does everyone do it?"

"Because your grandmother's generation believed the sound mattered. And because it's easier to avoid a number than to argue with your mother." He handed her chopsticks. "Give him fifty. Give him thirty-eight. Nobody at that booth is checking your math against the afterlife."

Maelie ate standing up, watching her grandmother across the street. The old woman had wedged herself onto a folding chair near the stage, where a lion costume was being readied by two teenagers, and she was handing out envelopes to the children of strangers, pressing them into palms with a formality that made the kids straighten up. She had been doing this since before the neighborhood was called a neighborhood, since the festival was a single folding table of sesame balls outside the grocery that had long since closed, its awning bleached and desiccated in old photographs on the wall of the dim sum place.

Maelie took out the two twenties and looked at them. Her father was right that the sound meant nothing, in the way that a word on a page meant nothing until someone read it. But her grandmother had stood in a bank line to get fresh bills because creased ones were careless, had bought the oranges with stems and leaves intact because bare fruit looked stripped, had done a hundred small exact things all morning without once explaining them. The point was not that four could hurt Dax. The point was that Dax, at nine, already knew the rule, and would notice if she broke it, and would file it somewhere as evidence about what her love was worth.

Still, she could hear her father too, and she did not want to pretend she couldn't. A number did not carry death the way a live wire carries current. If she gave forty and said nothing, nothing would happen. She took out her phone and texted Dax: forty-five okay? and watched him across the street, waiting at the goldfish booth with a paper bag, until he pulled his phone from his jacket, read it, and gave her a thumbs up so large his whole arm moved.

She re-stuffed the envelope with two twenties, a ten, and five ones, then folded it lengthwise and creased it with her thumbnail.

Her grandmother waved her over when the drums started. "Come, the lion is beginning. Bring the envelopes." Maelie crossed the street with the box of oranges and the red stack in her hands, and her grandmother pulled her down into the chair beside her and said, "Hold the money like this, both hands, when you give it. Never one hand."

"Okay," Maelie said, and turned the envelope over twice so the characters faced out.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
story:
The synagogue's social hall smelled of coffee and floor wax when Sienna arrived with three grocery bags and her grandmother's Haggadah boxed under one arm. Rabbi Fox had given her the key that afternoon, along with a clipboard listing what the families had signed up to bring, and Sienna had spent the drive rehearsing the order of the blessing over the candles, which she had only ever watched her grandfather recite. He was in hospice now, his voice down to a ribbon, and at Purim he had pressed the old book into her hands and said only, "You know more than you think."

She began by requisitioning the long folding tables from the storage closet, startling Mr. Adler, who was arranging chairs and who insisted on carrying the heavy ends himself. By six the hall had filled. Her parents came with her little brother, and her aunt and uncle, and then, hovering near the sign that said FIRST NIGHT SEDER, WELCOME, came a girl from Sienna's chem class named Priya, who had texted that morning asking if she could come because her roommate was away and the dorm was too quiet.

Sienna poured grape juice into the silver Kiddush cup and its paper-cup companions, and began. She stumbled on the second blessing, recovered, and felt her ears burn, but nobody laughed. Her little brother asked the Four Questions in a monotone that made Priya smile into her sleeve. When they reached the plate at the center of the table, Priya leaned toward it, curious and a little wary of the horseradish root and the shank bone and the pastel heap of charoset.

"That's maror," Sienna said. "Bitter herbs. Horseradish, usually. We eat them on purpose, to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt."

Priya looked at the root, then at the faces around the table. "You eat something bitter deliberately. At a party."

"At the exact opposite of a party," Sienna said. "Or the exact same thing. I've been arguing with myself about it all week." She held up the Haggadah, its spine cracked to softness. "My grandfather says the whole night is hermeneutics, that every generation has to read itself into the story, and for years I thought that was just something old men say to sound important. But tonight I keep catching myself doing it."

She distributed the maror, and Priya took her piece with the others, and Sienna watched her cousin Daniel, home from his first year of college and freshly bellicose about every tradition he'd grown up with, glare at the horseradish like it had personally insulted him. "This is performative suffering," he announced. "You can't taste someone else's slavery."

"You're not supposed to taste theirs," Sienna said. "You're supposed to notice what bitterness does in your own mouth, and then notice how fast you want it gone." She hadn't planned to say that. It came out of the week of reading, of the notes her grandfather had left in the margins in his cramped hand, and it landed in the room and sat there.

Daniel chewed his maror with theatrical resentment, eyes watering, and then said, unexpectedly, "Okay. That's actually not stupid." Priya's eyes were watering too, and she laughed while she cried, and Sienna's mother passed the charoset quickly down the table like a rescue line.

Later, after the meal, after the front door had been opened for Elijah and the night air had come in cold and smelling of rain, Sienna stood to lead the grace after the meal and found that her hands were steady. Daniel was humming along with the Chad Gadya under his breath, having declared it capitalist propaganda and then learned all six verses anyway. Priya had taken one of the extra Haggadot and was reading ahead, mouthing the words.

At the sink in the kitchen, washing the silver cup, Sienna thought about texting her grandfather a photo of the table. She typed and deleted three drafts. She didn't know yet whether she believed the way he believed, or whether the bitterness and the sweetness sat in any kind of order she could name, and she suspected she wouldn't know for years. What she knew was the cup in her hands and the sound of her family's voices carrying the last verses from the hall, and that seemed like enough to hold for one night.

She dried the cup, set it upright on the towel, and walked back in as they reached the final line, and she sang it louder than anyone.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
story:
Abigail would tell anyone who asked that she had never once been wrong in Mr. Ferreira's physics class, which was true only if you didn't count the midterm, the lab on pendulums, or the time she'd insisted that Venus was closer to Earth than Mars on average, which it is, but not for the reason she'd given. Today she had staked the whole period on being right again. She had asked Ferreira before class if she could present her independent project on the Higgs boson, and he had acceded with a shrug that suggested he expected very little, and that shrug was the thing she intended to make him regret.

The classroom smelled like the dust of chalk and the citrus of the spray they used on the whiteboards, and the radiator under the window ticked in a rhythm Abigail had memorized back in September, when she used to count the ticks instead of listening. Twenty-two desks. Nine students actually present, because it was the last week before exams and half the class had discovered that a signed field trip form was easier to obtain than a grasp of thermodynamics.

"Okay," she said, standing at the front with her laptop open on the demonstration bench. "So the Higgs boson. Discovered at CERN, announced July 4, 2012." She clicked to a slide she had spent two nights building, a photograph of a crowded auditorium with people standing along the walls. "Everyone always shows the particle. I want to show the room."

Rosa Delgado, who sat in the back and sardonic as a matter of policy, raised one eyebrow. "The room."

"The room matters," Abigail said, with more certainty than she felt, because she had only understood why the room mattered forty minutes ago, rereading the same paragraph in her kitchen while her mother asked twice whether she had eaten. "Look, here's what I used to think. I thought some team found a particle, and then there was a press conference, and that was it. Discovery, announcement, done. Like Newton and the apple, except with worse snacks." A small laugh from somewhere near the windows. Ferreira, at his desk, did not look up from his grading, which Abigail chose to interpret as respect.

She clicked again. Two photographs side by side, two enormous machines in underground caverns. "But CERN didn't have one giant detector looking for it. They had two. Two separate teams, completely independent of each other. ATLAS was one. CMS was the other. They weren't allowed to share their results while they worked, because if they compared notes, one team's result would contaminate the other's. You'd just have one answer wearing two coats." She heard herself say it and realized, with a strange double feeling, that she was teaching this to herself at the same time she was teaching it to them.

She remembered, then, her father at the science museum two summers ago, before he moved out, standing in front of a cutaway model of the collider with his arms crossed. A boy near them had asked the guide why CERN needed two giant detectors instead of one, and the guide had started to answer, and her father had said, loudly, "Because they didn't trust themselves, that's why," and laughed at his own joke, and the guide had said something polite about independent confirmation, and Abigail had been fifteen and embarrassed and had not listened. She had spent two years carrying around her father's version, certain of it, repeating it once at a party like it was hers. Standing in front of the class now, she understood that she had been confidently wrong, and that the wrongness had not even been hers. It was borrowed, secondhand, unexamined.

"That's the part that changed how I think about it," she said. "It's not that one experiment succeeded. It's that two teams, not sharing data, found the same new particle. Before July 4, 2012, nobody stood up and said it. Both teams had to get there first. Separately." She paused. "And even then, the announcement was the beginning of checking, not the end. Other physicists got the papers and went after the numbers. That's what the room was full of, in the photograph. People ready to take it apart."

Ferreira put his pen down. "So one result means nothing?"

"I didn't say nothing." She was careful now, slower. "One result means maybe. It means this happened once, in one machine, interpreted by one group of people who could all be making the same mistake together. Two independent results means probably. A hundred replications means we build the next thing on top of it." She looked at Rosa, who was no longer smirking. "I used to think science was a person being right. I think now it's more like a lot of people agreeing to try to prove you wrong, and the idea surviving anyway." She stopped, hearing the pedagogue in her own voice, the lecture-y drawl of someone who had read one book and become insufferable about it, and she added, quieter, "I might still be overselling it. I'm seventeen and my sources are a library database and a YouTube lecture with terrible audio."

Ferreira said, "That caveat is the most scientific thing you've said all period."

After class, Rosa caught her at the door. "My uncle works at a lab in Chicago," Rosa said. "He says they spend half their time trying to repeat other people's experiments and failing, and nobody publishes the failures, so we don't actually know how much falls apart. Does that break your whole speech?"

Abigail stood with her hand on the doorframe, the hallway noise swelling past them, lockers and sneakers and someone's tinny speaker. "No," she said. "It's just the part I can't see yet." Rosa shrugged, almost smiling, and walked off toward the stairwell. Abigail stayed a moment longer, looking at the empty room where two photographs of two machines still glowed on the screen, side by side in the dark, neither one knowing the other was there.

story:
The studio smelled of rosin and radiator dust, and the photocopy of Mozart's Sonata in C, K. 545, lay on the music rack with its margins already crowded. James had exhumed it from the bottom of his backpack that morning, smoothing the creases where his water bottle had flattened it for a week, and now Mrs. Okonkwo tapped the first system with her pencil.

"So. By Friday you hand me this movement with the exposition, the development and the recapitulation marked. Not colored. Marked, with reasons." She sat down in the chair by the window, the ascetic wooden one she never let students use because it threw her back out, and folded her hands. "Show me where you are."

"I found the second theme," James said, and played the run of sixteenths in the right hand, the bright climbing figure he'd been noodling for days. "Here. That's the second theme, so the first theme has to end somewhere before it, right? But I don't know where. The whole first page just sounds like one long idea."

"Then you don't know where the second theme starts either," Mrs. Okonkwo said. "You know where something you like starts."

He hated when she did that, reframed his answer so it became a smaller answer, and he stared at the page as if the barlines might confess. The trouble was that the beginning was cheerful, then more cheerful, then cheerfully busier, and he couldn't point to a moment and say this is new. He had skipped the busy part all week when he practiced, hands leaping over it to land on the tune he liked. The awkward passage was an externality, a debt he kept pushing onto some future James who would have to pay it, and future James had apparently arrived.

"Play from the top," Mrs. Okonkwo said. "Slowly. And listen to your left hand for once in your life."

He played. The opening chords sat under his fingers like home, C major, plain as a kitchen table, and the melody wandered away from them and came back. Then, eight bars or so in, the texture changed. The right hand stopped singing and started working, sixteenths tumbling over each other, nothing you could whistle. And underneath, almost sneaky, the harmonies shifted. He slowed further and the left hand's F natural gave way to F sharp, and something lifted, the whole floor of the music tilting toward G.

"Stop," he said to himself, and did stop, hands hovering. "That's it. That's where it changes key."

"Changes from what to what?" Mrs. Okonkwo asked, and she was not being sarcastic, which somehow made it worse.

"From C to G. The dominant." He traced the bars with his pencil. "So this passage here, the busy part, it's not part of the first theme and it's not the second theme. It's the thing that gets you from one to the other." He hesitated, then remembered the word from a video he'd watched at midnight with his headphones on. "The transition. Some people call it the bridge."

"Mm," said Mrs. Okonkwo, which from her was applause. "And what is it made of, this bridge? What kind of material?"

He looked again at the tumbling sixteenths, the two bars where the melody turned into arithmetic. "Busy stuff," he said. "Not tuneful. It's like he didn't want you to remember it, he just wanted you to end up in the new key and be surprised the tune sounds different there." He wrote TRANSITION in the margin, boxed it, and underneath, smaller: busier, less tuneful, changes key. Then he bracketed the first theme before it, and after the bridge the second theme finally had a birth certificate instead of just a vibe.

"Good. Now the question you should be asking." She stood and came to the piano. "The exposition ends and the development begins, and you will find that easier, because the development sounds unsettled, it wanders. The recapitulation is where he comes home." She turned toward the last page. "Friday. And James, you may not skip the bridge when you practice. You skipped it all week, I could hear the hole in your playing from the waiting room."

He felt his ears go hot. "How did you know I skipped it?"

"Because you played it today like a man walking through a doorway he's afraid of." She laughed once, short, and gathered her coffee mug. "The bridge is the door. Everything interesting happens when you decide to go through it."

At home that night he spread the score across the kitchen table and worked with a ruler and three colors, and the movement organized itself under his hands like a city getting street signs. First theme, bridge, second theme, closing section; then the long unsettled middle; then the return. When he came to the recapitulation he sat back, satisfied, and started bracketing the return of the first theme in the last third of the page. Home again, C major, plain as a kitchen table.

Then he reached the place where the bridge had been before, the busy tumbling passage, and his pencil stopped in the air. He played it. Sixteenths, busier than anything around them, exactly the door he had learned to recognize, and this time he listened hard for the tilt, for the F sharp, for the floor lifting toward a new key.

It never came. The harmonies churned and settled and stayed exactly, stubbornly, in C. He played it three times, then checked the key signature twice, then leaned over the page until his nose nearly touched the print, wondering whether Mozart had made a mistake, whether he had, whether a bridge could still be a bridge if it went nowhere, if the whole point of coming home was that the door could look the same and open onto the same room.

He texted Mrs. Okonkwo, which he never did: "the recap bridge doesn't change key. is that allowed?" He sat with his chin on his fists, staring at the boxed word TRANSITION in the margin of the second half, which now looked less like a label and more like a question, and his phone buzzed once on the table.

She had replied with a single line: "What do you think the second theme sounds like in C instead of G?"

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
story:
The problem on the worksheet gave the charge on each plate, the area of each plate, and nothing else, and Grace read it three times before she understood that the omission was deliberate. Mr. Okafor had written the voltage on the board for every other problem, a tidy given like a handrail, and now he had taken it away. Across the lab, Dara was already flipping through her notes with the frantic efficiency of someone who intended to find the answer before admitting she had lost it. Grace looked down at her own page, where she had copied the numbers in her small careful hand: so many coulombs, so many square metres.

"You can't get the field without the voltage," Dara said, not looking up. "That's the whole formula. E equals V over d. It's literally the formula."

"Then why would he give us this one?"

"Because he's testing whether we'll admit it's impossible. It's a trick." Dara said this with the certainty of someone who had been tricked before and had decided never to be tricked again, and Grace envied the certainty more than she believed it. Mr. Okafor did not write tricks. He wrote problems that looked impossible until you turned them over.

She turned it over. The plates were ideal, the sheet said, parallel and infinite, which meant the field between them was uniform, which meant the voltage formula was one way of describing something that could be described other ways. She thought of her mother suturing a hem, drawing two edges of fabric together so the seam held without a knot showing; there was always more than one stitch that would hold a thing closed. Charge was given. Area was given. Charge divided by area was something she could compute, a density, the crowding of charge on the plate. And if the crowding of charge was what made the field, then the field ought to come out of that density somehow, divided by some constant of the universe she half remembered seeing in the back of the textbook, unexplained and mysterious as a vestigial organ, printed in a table of constants she had never once used.

She found it in the reference page, between c and h: the permittivity of free space, 8.85 × 10^-12 farads per metre. The symbol was epsilon with a subscript zero, and the table offered no apology for it. Dara leaned over her shoulder.

"What's that?"

"Permittivity of free space," Grace said. "It's in the constants table. About eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve farads per metre."

"So the field is the charge per area divided by that?"

"That's what I'm going to try." She tried it. She wrote the density first, the charge divided by the plate's area, and then she divided that by the tiny stubborn number, and the answer that emerged was a field strength in newtons per coulomb, plausible and clean, the kind of number that Mr. Okafor's problems always produced when you had done the thing he wanted you to do. She sat back and looked at it and did not trust it, because it had arrived by a road she had never walked before.

Dara did it too, in her own handwriting, and got the same number, and still looked unsatisfied. "But how do we know this isn't just a formula that happens to work for this problem? Like, what if he wants the other way?"

"He can want both ways. They're both true. One uses the voltage, one uses the charge on the plates." Grace tapped the page. "If he'd given us the voltage, we'd never have needed this. Maybe that's why he left it out." She heard how it sounded when she said it, like clemency extended to a man who had withheld the voltage on purpose, as if the omission were not a cruelty but a door, and she decided she meant it that way. She was less sure about the deeper thing, whether the two formulas were two descriptions of one field or two fields that happened to coincide, and she wrote a question mark in the margin next to her answer and let it stand.

Mr. Okafor came by on his slow circuit of the room, looked at her page without touching it, and moved on, which was his version of a nod. Dara erased nothing, copied the answer onto the final line, and snapped her binder shut. At the end of the period, Grace stayed behind a moment to write the question from the margin onto the worksheet itself, below the answer, where he would be sure to see it: how do we know the two methods agree when we can't check both? She left the paper in the center of the bench, squared to its edge, and the question mark inked dark and visible at the bottom of the page.

activity: getting a first part-time job
story:
Tristan had never been wrong about arithmetic, and he told himself this the way other people told themselves they were brave. So when he opened his first envelope from Halvorsen's Hardware and found sixty-eight dollars and change where seventy-three should have been, he assumed the fault lay with the envelope, or with Mr. Halvorsen, or with the wrinkled old man who did the books, and not with the only certainty he owned.

He had worked eleven hours at six sixty-five an hour. He had done the math twice on the walk home, once more at the kitchen table, and a fourth time in the margin of the flyer announcing the store's summer inventory sale, which started Saturday. Saturday was also the deadline to sign the rest of his hiring paperwork, the forms still folded in his backpack, and Mr. Halvorsen had said, in his flat way, that if the papers were not in by then, the job would go to the Rennick boy, who was fifteen and, according to everyone, unemployable.

Tristan's mother said eleven times six sixty-five was seventy-three fifteen, which settled nothing, since he already knew that. His sister said stores steal from kids, which he found too easy. Only Dee, who ran the register on weekends and had worked at Halvorsen's since she was fourteen herself, might know something, so Friday afternoon, with the paperwork deadline a day away and his suspicion calcifying into a grievance, he took his envelope to the register and laid it flat between them.

"Shorted," he said. He said it quietly, the way you say a word you have rehearsed. "Eleven hours. I counted."

Dee did not look impressed. She looked, if anything, tired, and she pulled her own check stub from under the register mat, where she kept it as though it were a bookmark for a book she had stopped reading. "Employers withhold part of your wages," she said. "Six point two percent, for Social Security tax. Up to a yearly wage limit, then it stops for the year."

Tristan looked at the stub, then at his own envelope, then at the ceiling fan turning its slow circles over aisle three. Six point two percent of seventy-three fifteen was four dollars and fifty-three cents, give or take a penny, and seventy-three fifteen minus four fifty-three was sixty-eight sixty-two, which was the number in the envelope down to the last digit. He had been shorted nothing. The ground he had stood on all week, the solid arithmetic ground, had been arithmetic about the wrong thing.

He thought about Mr. Halvorsen, whom he had privately cast as the villain, a man with detractors all over town who claimed he watered down the paint and fired boys for looking at their phones. Tristan had believed them, he realized, because the story fit the number, and the number fit the story, and neither had been checked against the other. It was a profligate way to spend a certainty, handing it out to anyone who would take it, and he had been doing it all week.

"You could have said something," he told Dee, though even as he said it he heard how it sounded, like a boy who wanted the world to apologize for arithmetic.

"You could have asked," Dee said. She rang up a woman buying curtain rods and did not look at him until the receipt was torn. "Most kids don't. They just quit and tell everyone they got robbed, and then the Rennick boy gets the job and the town gets another story about Halvorsen's." She slid the stub back under the mat. "I did that my first month. Told my dad the old man was a thief. He made me sit down with the numbers."

"Was he right to?"

"He made me figure it out myself. That part was right." She straightened the pens by the register, five of them, none of which wrote. "The part where I already knew he'd say I told you so, that part I made up. I'm still not sure which part was worse, what I got wrong or how sure I was while I was getting it wrong."

Tristan picked up his envelope. He did not feel corrected so much as rearranged, as though the store had shifted its aisles overnight and he was still navigating by the old map. Somewhere between his certainty and the town's stories about the old man was a version of things he could actually verify, and it was smaller than either, and slower, and it did not come with the satisfaction of knowing whom to blame.

He walked the three blocks home in the flattening light, took the forms from his backpack, and signed every page at the kitchen table. Then, before he could lose his nerve, he did the math on what Saturday's hours would come to, the gross and the withheld part, both numbers, in pencil, so he could change them.

At the store the next morning he handed the paperwork to Mr. Halvorsen, who looked at it longer than a stack of signatures seemed to require. "Sixty-eight sixty-two," Tristan said. "Last week. It checked out." The old man grunted and filed the papers in a drawer that stuck, and Dee, restocking near the register, said, "Told you nobody robbed him."
